Antibiotics usually arrive as short recall inside a disease question (name the drug for a bacterial infection) and, on Unit 7 Booklet B, as plates with clear zones: which antibiotic works best and why, in comparative words, and the minimum effective concentration (Summer 2019, 2023, 2025). Resistance and superbugs are Higher only: a diagram of a dish before and after an antibiotic, an MRSA graph with true, false or cannot-tell statements, and procedures to reduce spread (Summer 2023, 2024, 2025). Vaccination questions ask what the vaccine raises and why the second response is faster; Higher papers add an antibody graph with a booster (Summer 2021).

noteBlocks.lede: Two ways to beat a pathogen: kill it with a drug, or train your body before it arrives. Antibiotics do the first, for bacteria only, and overusing them breeds bacteria they cannot kill. Vaccines do the second, by leaving memory behind.
can: Explain what antibiotics do, why they fail against viruses, and read a plate of clear zones.
Explain resistance as natural selection, and how hospitals keep superbugs such as MRSA down.
Describe how a vaccine and a booster protect you, and read an antibody graph.

noteBlocks.caption: An antibiotic acts on a part only bacteria have. A virus inside one of your cells offers it nothing.

noteBlocks.md: An **antibiotic** is a chemical made by fungi, such as **penicillin**, used against diseases caused by bacteria. It either **kills the bacteria** or **slows their growth**. Many antibiotics attack the cell wall, which only bacteria have, as in the drawing. A virus has no cell wall and reproduces inside your own cells, so antibiotics do nothing against colds, flu or HIV.

Penicillin is an antibiotic: a fungus makes it, and a patient can take it to kill bacteria inside the body. The alcohol in hand gel is not one: it kills bacteria on skin, but no fungus makes it, and nobody could take it as a medicine.

noteBlocks.title: Antibiotic or antibody?
noteBlocks.md: An **antibiotic** is the drug, made by fungi. An **antibody** is a protein your own lymphocytes make. Examiners have found antibodies written where the drug is meant, so match the word to the question.

noteBlocks.stem: A doctor sees two patients, one with chlamydia and one with HIV. Explain why she prescribes an antibiotic for only one of them.

steps.working: Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium, so an antibiotic can kill it: she prescribes one.
steps.decision: Start with the pathogen. A bacterium has the cell wall that many antibiotics attack.

steps.working: HIV is a virus: it has no cell wall and reproduces inside the patient's own cells.
steps.decision: Give the reason, not just the type: there is nothing for the antibiotic to act on.

steps.working: So an antibiotic would do nothing against HIV, which is slowed with antiviral drugs instead.
steps.decision: End on what the question asked: why one patient gets it and the other does not.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these diseases could be treated with an antibiotic?
options: tuberculosis
flu
a cold
noteBlocks.explain: Ask what causes each one, as See it did: an antibiotic acts only on bacteria. Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium; flu and colds are caused by viruses, which reproduce inside your own cells. The answer is tuberculosis.

twin.explain: Salmonella is a bacterium, so an antibiotic can kill it. HPV and flu are viruses, which antibiotics cannot touch. The answer is salmonella food poisoning.

optionNotes.option: HPV

optionNotes.option: flu
optionNotes.why: Flu makes people ill enough to ask for antibiotics, but it is caused by a virus, which antibiotics cannot touch.

optionNotes.option: flu
optionNotes.why: Flu can make you feel ill enough to want a strong drug, but it is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only act on bacteria.

optionNotes.option: a cold
optionNotes.why: Colds are so common that antibiotics look like the obvious fix, but a cold is a virus, with no cell wall for an antibiotic to attack.

noteBlocks.caption: Where an antibiotic works, it clears a zone in the lawn of bacteria. The wider the zone, the more bacteria it killed.

noteBlocks.md: To compare antibiotics, bacteria are spread over agar, paper discs soaked in different antibiotics are laid on top, and the dish is incubated for a few days. Round a disc that works, the bacteria die and leave a **clear zone**. The **larger** the clear zone, the **more effective** that antibiotic is against these bacteria.

**No clear zone** means that antibiotic killed none of these bacteria, for one of two reasons: the dose on the disc was too weak, or the bacteria are **resistant** to it. One plate on its own cannot tell you which.

noteBlocks.title: Say which is biggest
noteBlocks.md: On the Summer 2025 practical paper, most candidates picked the right antibiotic, but many lost the marks for the reason. The reason needs the comparison in words: it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria.

noteBlocks.stem: A student tests streptomycin, penicillin and tetracycline, at the same concentration, on one plate of bacteria. The clear zones are 21 mm, 8 mm and none. Describe and explain the results.

steps.working: Streptomycin was the most effective: it had the largest clear zone, 21 mm, so it killed the most bacteria.
steps.decision: Name it, compare with a word ending in -est, and quote the evidence: 'a big zone' fits any disc that has one.

steps.working: Penicillin had a smaller clear zone, 8 mm, so it killed fewer bacteria.
steps.decision: Every result gets a sentence, and each one says what its zone means.

steps.working: Tetracycline had no clear zone, so it killed none: either it was too weak at this concentration, or these bacteria are resistant to it.
steps.decision: No zone has two possible causes, and one plate cannot separate them, so give both.

noteBlocks.prompt: On one plate, antibiotic A gives a clear zone 26 mm across, antibiotic B one 15 mm across, and antibiotic C none. Which answer earns the marks for choosing the most effective antibiotic?
options: A, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria
A, because it had a big clear zone
C, because the bacteria grew right up to it
noteBlocks.answer: A, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria
noteBlocks.explain: A clear zone is where bacteria were killed, so the widest zone marks the antibiotic that killed the most. With three to compare, 'a big clear zone' could describe any of them: the mark needs 'largest' and what it means. C killed none. The answer is A, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria.

twin.prompt: On another plate, antibiotic P gives a clear zone 12 mm across, Q one 19 mm across and R one 4 mm across. Which answer earns the marks for choosing the most effective antibiotic?
options: Q, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria
Q, because it had a big clear zone
R, because its clear zone was the smallest
twin.answer: Q, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria
twin.explain: The widest clear zone marks the antibiotic that killed the most, and the mark needs the comparison, 'largest', with what it means. R's small zone shows it killed the fewest. The answer is Q, because it had the largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria.

optionNotes.option: Q, because it had a big clear zone
optionNotes.why: It picks the right antibiotic, but 'big' is not a comparison: with three zones the mark needs 'largest', then that it killed the most.

optionNotes.option: R, because its clear zone was the smallest
optionNotes.why: The smallest zone means R killed the fewest bacteria, so it is the least effective, not the most.

optionNotes.option: A, because it had a big clear zone
optionNotes.why: It picks the right antibiotic, but 'big' is not a comparison: with three discs the mark needs 'largest', then that it killed the most.

optionNotes.option: C, because the bacteria grew right up to it
optionNotes.why: Bacteria growing right up to a disc means that antibiotic killed none of them, so C is the least effective, not the best.

noteBlocks.md: Scientists also test **one** antibiotic at a range of concentrations. Below a certain concentration it kills nothing, so its disc has no clear zone. The **minimum effective concentration** is the lowest concentration that still gives a clear zone: the weakest dose that works.
It matters because a patient given no more antibiotic than is needed has fewer side effects, and using less cuts the overuse that lets resistant bacteria spread.

noteBlocks.stem: Use the strip in the figure to find the minimum effective concentration of this antibiotic, and explain your answer.

steps.working: The discs at 1 and 2 units have no clear zone.
steps.decision: Start at the weakest end: at these concentrations the antibiotic killed none of the bacteria.

steps.working: The disc at 4 units is the first with a clear zone, and the smallest, 6 mm.
steps.decision: The smallest zone of the ones that have one: it killed the fewest bacteria, but it still worked.

steps.working: So the minimum effective concentration is 4 units.
steps.decision: The lowest concentration with a zone: not the lowest on the strip, and not the one with the biggest zone.

noteBlocks.prompt: Another antibiotic is tested on discs of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 units. Only the discs at 40 and 80 units have clear zones. What is its minimum effective concentration, in units? Give the number only.
noteBlocks.explain: Find the lowest concentration that still clears a zone, as See it did: the discs at 5, 10 and 20 units killed nothing, and 40 units is the first that worked. Higher concentrations work too, but they are not the minimum. The answer is 40.

twin.prompt: A third antibiotic is tested at 3, 6, 12 and 24 units. Every disc except the one at 3 units has a clear zone. What is its minimum effective concentration, in units? Give the number only.
twin.explain: The disc at 3 units has no zone, so it killed nothing; 6 units is the lowest concentration that still worked. The answer is 6.

noteBlocks.caption: Each dose kills most of the bacteria that are not resistant; the resistant ones survive and multiply.

noteBlocks.md: In any population of bacteria there is **variation**: by chance, a **mutation** makes a few resistant to an antibiotic. The antibiotic kills most of the bacteria that are not resistant. The resistant ones **survive**, **reproduce** and pass on the gene for resistance, so each dose raises the share that is resistant. Every time antibiotics are **overused**, it happens again, until the antibiotic hardly works.

noteBlocks.title: Why it is selection, not immunity
noteBlocks.md: Bacteria have no immune system and make no antibodies. The antibiotic does not create resistance either: the resistant bacteria were there before it was used. It only removes the others, which leaves the resistant ones to multiply.

steps.working: Each dose killed most of the bacteria that were not resistant, and the resistant ones survived.
steps.decision: Say which ones were killed and which survived: the resistant ones were never killed.

steps.working: The survivors reproduced and passed on the gene for resistance, so each generation held more resistant bacteria.
steps.decision: The last link is inheritance: without it, nothing explains the next generation.

noteBlocks.caption: Four ways a ward cuts the spread of MRSA, and how each one works.

noteBlocks.md: A **superbug** is a bacterium resistant to most antibiotics, such as **MRSA**. Flu is not a superbug, even though antibiotics fail against it: it is a virus, which antibiotics never acted on. Superbugs are hard to get rid of because few antibiotics treat them, they spread on hands, clothes and surfaces, some people carry them without being ill, and hospital patients are often already weak.

So wards block the spread. **Washing hands** between patients removes bacteria; **alcohol gel**, antiseptics and disinfectants kill them outside the body. **Isolating** a patient in a side room means fewer contacts, and **gloves** and aprons are a barrier. Prescribing antibiotics only when they are needed slows new resistance.

noteBlocks.stem: A patient on a ward has MRSA. Explain how each of these reduces its spread: the nurse washes her hands between patients, the patient is moved to a side room, and staff wear gloves and an apron.

steps.working: Washing her hands between patients removes MRSA bacteria from her skin, so she does not carry them to the next bed.
steps.decision: Washing takes bacteria off; it is not the step that kills them.

steps.working: In a side room the patient meets fewer people, so fewer can pick the bacteria up and pass them on.
steps.decision: Isolation works on the route, not on the bacteria themselves.

steps.working: Gloves and an apron keep the bacteria off the staff's skin and clothes, and are thrown away before the next patient.
steps.decision: A barrier stops the bacteria riding on staff from one patient to another.

to treat the patients who already have MRSA
noteBlocks.answer: to kill the MRSA bacteria left on surfaces people touch
noteBlocks.explain: A disinfectant kills bacteria outside the body, and MRSA resists only antibiotics, so it dies too. Surfaces carry bacteria from hand to hand, the route See it blocked with washing and gloves. Disinfecting cannot treat anyone already ill. The answer is to kill the MRSA left on surfaces people touch.

noteBlocks.md: A **vaccine** contains a **modified** form of a pathogen, dead or weakened, so it cannot make you ill, but it carries the **same antigens** as the real one. **Lymphocytes**, a kind of white blood cell, recognise those antigens and make **antibodies**, and some become **memory lymphocytes**, which stay in the blood. So a vaccine raises the levels of antibodies and memory lymphocytes.

When the real pathogen arrives, the memory lymphocytes recognise it at once, so antibodies are made **faster** and in **greater numbers** than the first time, and the pathogen is destroyed before you feel ill. Vaccines matter most against viruses, which are hard to treat, but some protect against bacteria, such as tetanus.

An injection of ready-made antibodies against tetanus, given after a deep cut, is **not** a vaccine: it protects at once, but only for a short time, because no memory lymphocytes are made. A vaccine protects for years.

noteBlocks.stem: Orla was given the measles vaccine, which contains weakened measles viruses, as a baby. Years later measles spreads through her class. Explain why she stays well while an unvaccinated classmate becomes ill.

steps.working: The weakened viruses in the vaccine could not make her ill, but they carried the same antigens as real measles viruses.
steps.decision: Start with what was injected: harmless, but recognisable.

steps.working: Her lymphocytes made antibodies against them, and memory lymphocytes that stayed in her blood.
steps.decision: The memory lymphocytes are the part that lasts for years.

steps.working: When real measles viruses get in, her memory lymphocytes recognise their antigens at once.
steps.decision: Recognition is immediate the second time: nothing has to be learned again.

steps.working: Antibodies are made faster and in greater numbers, so the viruses are destroyed before she is ill; her classmate's first response is too slow.
steps.decision: Two marks sit here, faster and more: say both, then say what that means for the pathogen.

noteBlocks.explain: A vaccine makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory lymphocytes, as Orla's did in See it. noteBlocks.md: Over time the level of antibodies in the blood falls. A **booster** is a second dose of the same vaccine: it meets memory lymphocytes, so antibodies are made **faster**, reach a **higher** level and go on being made for **longer** than after the first dose. On an antibody graph a dashed line marks the level needed for **immunity**: the person is protected only while the curve is above it.

Two calculations come up. **How many times higher**: divide the larger peak by the smaller. **For how long**: subtract the week the curve crosses the line going up from the week it crosses going down.

noteBlocks.stem: Use the graph in the figure to give three differences between the responses to the first dose and to the booster, then calculate how many times higher the booster's peak is.

steps.working: Faster: after the booster the level passes the dashed line within a week; after the first dose it never reaches it.
steps.decision: Compare how steeply each curve rises.

steps.working: Higher: the peaks are 16 after the first dose and 144 after the booster.
steps.decision: Read each peak straight across to the scale, and say what you read.

steps.working: Longer: the level stays above the line from just after week 12 to week 26, about 14 weeks; after the first dose, never.
steps.decision: Subtract the two weeks where the curve crosses the line: 26 − 12.

steps.working: 144 ÷ 16 = 9, so the booster's peak is 9 times higher.
steps.decision: 'How many times' is a division: 144 − 16 = 128 says how much higher, a different question.

noteBlocks.prompt: On another antibody graph, the peak after a booster is 90 arbitrary units and the peak after the first dose is 15. How many times higher is the booster's peak?
noteBlocks.explain: 'How many times higher' is a division of the larger peak by the smaller, as step 4 of See it did, never a subtraction: 90 − 15 = 75 says how much higher, not how many times. 90 ÷ 15 = 6.

twin.prompt: A third graph has peaks of 10 after the first dose and 80 after the booster. How many times higher is the booster's peak?
twin.explain: Divide the larger peak by the smaller: 80 ÷ 10 = 8. Subtracting gives 70, which is how much higher, not how many times. The answer is 8.

items.stem: In natural selection, which individuals are most likely to survive and reproduce?

options.text: those best suited to their environment
options.feedback: The best-suited survive and pass on their alleles. Antibiotic resistance is the same idea, happening fast.
Size only helps if it suits the conditions. 'Best suited to the environment' is the idea.

options.text: those that try hardest to adapt
options.feedback: No organism chooses to adapt. Individuals that happen to be suited survive.
Age has nothing to do with it. The best-suited survive and reproduce.

options.text: A chemical made by fungi that kills bacteria or stops them growing
options.feedback: Exactly: penicillin, from a mould, is the classic example.

options.text: A protein made by white blood cells that sticks to antigens
options.feedback: That is an antibody. An antibiotic is a drug.

options.text: A weakened form of a pathogen that gives immunity
options.feedback: That is a vaccine.
Antibiotics do not affect viruses at all.

items.stem: Why are antibiotics no use against flu?
items.skill: Explain why antibiotics fail on viruses

options.text: Flu is caused by a virus, which antibiotics do not affect
options.feedback: Right: antibiotics act only on bacteria.

options.text: The flu bacteria are all resistant
options.feedback: Flu is not bacterial; it is caused by a virus.

options.text: Flu is too mild to need them
options.feedback: Even severe flu is not treated with antibiotics, because it is a virus.

options.text: The flu vaccine stops them working
options.feedback: Vaccines and antibiotics do not interfere. Flu is viral.

items.stem: Higher Tier. How does a population of bacteria become resistant to an antibiotic?

options.text: Resistant bacteria already present survive the antibiotic and reproduce
options.feedback: Selection, not change: the resistant ones were there first.

options.text: The bacteria make antibodies against the antibiotic
options.feedback: Bacteria have no immune system. This is natural selection, not immunity.

options.text: Each bacterium gets used to the antibiotic and changes
options.feedback: No individual changes. Resistant bacteria were already there, and the antibiotic removed the rest.

options.text: The antibiotic mutates the bacteria it touches
options.feedback: Mutations happen by chance, before the antibiotic. It only selects which bacteria survive.

items.stem: Higher Tier. What makes MRSA a superbug?

options.text: It is resistant to most antibiotics
options.feedback: That is the definition: most antibiotics no longer kill it.

options.text: It is a virus, so antibiotics cannot reach it
options.feedback: MRSA is a bacterium. It is resistant, not viral.

options.text: It cannot be killed by any chemical
options.feedback: Alcohol gel, antiseptics and disinfectants kill it outside the body; that is how hospitals control it.

options.text: It grows much larger than other bacteria
options.feedback: Size is not the issue. It is resistant to most antibiotics.

options.text: A modified form of the pathogen, such as a dead or weakened one
options.feedback: Enough to be recognised, not enough to make you ill.
The body makes its own antibodies in response. A vaccine contains a modified pathogen.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections; they are not in vaccines.
Memory lymphocytes are made by your body after the vaccine, not put in by it.

items.stem: Higher Tier. Why is a booster vaccination given?
items.skill: Explain the role of a booster

options.text: To raise antibody and memory lymphocyte levels again as they fall
options.feedback: A booster tops the levels back up, usually well above the level needed for immunity.

options.text: To cure the disease if the first dose did not work
options.feedback: A booster prevents; it does not cure.

options.text: Because the first dose contained no antigens
options.feedback: The first dose did contain antigens; the levels it produced simply fall over time.

options.text: To kill bacteria that survived the first dose
options.feedback: Vaccines do not kill bacteria directly. A booster raises antibody and memory lymphocyte levels.

items.stem: Higher Tier. A dish holds mostly non-resistant bacteria and a few resistant ones. An antibiotic that kills every non-resistant bacterium is added. What will the dish hold 24 hours later?

options.text: Only resistant bacteria, and more of them than before
options.feedback: The antibiotic removed every non-resistant one; the resistant ones kept dividing.

options.text: Mostly non-resistant bacteria, with a few more resistant ones
options.feedback: An antibiotic that kills every non-resistant bacterium leaves none of them behind. Only the resistant ones remain, and they multiply.
The resistant bacteria are not killed, so they survive and multiply.

options.text: The same bacteria as before, now all resistant
options.feedback: No bacterium changes. The resistant ones were there from the start; the others were killed.

items.stem: Why is the second response to the same pathogen so fast?

options.text: Memory lymphocytes recognise it and antibodies are made quickly
options.feedback: Memory cells, faster, more: the three ideas every mark scheme looks for.

options.text: The antibodies have exactly the right shape for the antigen
options.feedback: They always do. What makes the second time faster is the memory lymphocytes.

options.text: The pathogen is weaker the second time
options.feedback: The pathogen is just as strong; the body is better prepared.
The memory belongs to memory lymphocytes.

context.setting: What antibiotics are, where they come from and what they do

parts.stem: Name one antibiotic.

accepted: penicillin

scheme.for: penicillin (or another named antibiotic)

hints: The first one was found growing in a mould.
parts.workedSolution: Penicillin.

commonErrors.feedback: Antibodies are made by your own lymphocytes. An antibiotic is a drug: penicillin is the one to name.

parts.stem: Penicillin is made by a type of microorganism. Name the type.

accepted: a fungus

scheme.for: fungus / fungi / mould

hints: The same kind of organism as athlete's foot and potato blight.
parts.workedSolution: A fungus (a mould called Penicillium).

parts.stem: Name the type of pathogen that antibiotics are used against.

accepted: bacteria

scheme.for: bacteria

hints: Not viruses, and not fungi.
parts.workedSolution: Bacteria.

commonErrors.feedback: Antibiotics have no effect on viruses. They are used against bacteria only.

parts.stem: Give the two ways an antibiotic can affect the bacteria it is used against.

accepted: it kills them, or it stops them growing

any: slow down the bacteria from growing
slow down the bacteria from multiplying
slow down the bacteria from reproducing
slow down the bacteria from dividing

scheme.for: kills the bacteria
stops or reduces their growth

hints: One is final; the other only holds them back.
parts.workedSolution: An antibiotic either kills the bacteria or stops them growing.

parts.stem: Which of these is a chemical made by lymphocytes that sticks to a pathogen's antigens?

options.feedback: An antibody: your own lymphocytes make it.
An antibiotic is a drug, made by a fungus or in a factory. Your lymphocytes make antibodies.
A vaccine is given by injection; it contains a modified pathogen, not antibodies.

scheme.for: antibody

parts.workedSolution: An antibody.

parts.stem: Which of these is a chemical made by fungi that kills bacteria or stops them growing?

options.feedback: Antibodies come from your own lymphocytes. The chemical made by fungi is an antibiotic.
An antibiotic, such as penicillin.
A vaccine prepares the body in advance; it does not kill bacteria itself.

scheme.for: antibiotic

parts.workedSolution: An antibiotic.

parts.stem: Which of these contains a modified form of a disease-causing organism?

options.feedback: An antibody is a chemical your body makes, not a form of the pathogen.
An antibiotic is a drug; it contains no pathogen.
A vaccine: a dead, weakened or otherwise modified pathogen.

scheme.for: vaccine

parts.workedSolution: A vaccine.

context.setting: What a vaccine contains and what it does

parts.stem: What does a vaccine contain?

accepted: a modified form of the pathogen, such as a dead or weakened one

scheme.for: a modified / dead / weakened (form of the) pathogen, or its antigens

hints: Enough of the pathogen to be recognised, not enough to make you ill.
parts.workedSolution: A modified form of the disease-causing organism, such as a dead or weakened one.

commonErrors.feedback: A vaccine contains no antibodies or antibiotics: it contains a modified form of the pathogen, and your own lymphocytes then make the antibodies.

parts.stem: Name two things whose levels rise in the blood after a vaccination.

accepted: antibodies and memory lymphocytes

scheme.for: antibodies
memory lymphocytes / memory cells

hints: One is a chemical; the other is a kind of white blood cell.
parts.workedSolution: Antibodies and memory lymphocytes.

commonErrors.feedback: Antibiotics are drugs; the body does not make them. After a vaccine, the levels that rise are antibodies and memory lymphocytes.

parts.stem: Some months after being vaccinated, a person is infected by the real pathogen but does not become ill. Explain why.

accepted: memory lymphocytes recognise the pathogen, so antibodies are made faster and in greater numbers, and it is destroyed before symptoms appear

scheme.for: memory lymphocytes (from the vaccine) recognise the pathogen
antibodies are produced faster
in greater numbers (or for longer), so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms

hints: Three ideas: who remembers, how fast, how many.
parts.workedSolution: Memory lymphocytes made after the vaccine recognise the pathogen's antigens, so antibodies are produced much faster and in greater numbers than the first time, and the pathogen is destroyed before it can cause symptoms.

commonErrors.feedback: That is why an antibody works, not why the second response wins. The marks are for memory lymphocytes, antibodies made faster, and more of them.

context.setting: A patient with a cold asks for antibiotics

parts.stem: A patient with a cold asks her doctor for antibiotics. The doctor refuses. Explain why.

accepted: a cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only kill bacteria

scheme.for: a cold is caused by a virus
antibiotics only kill bacteria / have no effect on viruses

hints: Two sentences: what causes a cold, and what antibiotics can act on.
parts.workedSolution: A cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only kill bacteria, so they would do nothing to help her.

commonErrors.feedback: A cold is caused by a virus, not a bacterium, which is exactly why antibiotics cannot help.

context.setting: Choosing the most effective of three antibiotics from repeated measurements

data.caption: Clear-zone diameters for three antibiotics against one bacterium

parts.stem:
A student measured the clear zone round discs of three antibiotics, J, K and L, three times each. The table shows her results.
Calculate the mean clear-zone diameter for antibiotic L. Give your answer to one decimal place.
hints: Add the three repeats first, then divide the total by 3; brackets make the calculator do it in that order.

commonErrors.feedback: The calculator divided only the last repeat by 3, because there were no brackets. A mean always lies between the smallest and largest repeat, so 57.3 mm cannot be right. Type (26 + 23 + 25) ÷ 3.
That is the total of the three repeats. The mean is the total divided by the number of repeats, 3.

parts.stem: Which antibiotic was the most effective against this bacterium?

options.feedback: J has the smallest mean clear zone, 10.0 mm.
K's mean, 18.0 mm, is smaller than L's.
L: its mean clear zone, 24.7 mm, is the largest.

scheme.for: L

parts.workedSolution: Antibiotic L.

parts.stem: Explain your answer, using the means.

accepted: L had the largest mean clear zone, 24.7 mm

more than both j and k

hints: Compare: which mean is the largest?
parts.workedSolution: L had the largest mean clear zone, 24.7 mm, compared with 18.0 mm for K and 10.0 mm for J, so it killed the most bacteria.

commonErrors.feedback: A comparison needs a comparing word: L had the largest mean clear zone.

parts.stem: By what percentage did the number of patients per 10 000 developing MRSA in hospital A fall between 2016 and 2021? Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.stem:
The graph shows how the level of antibodies in one person's blood changed after a first dose of a vaccine and a booster.
Use the graph to give the highest antibody level reached after the first dose.

scheme.for: 20 (arbitrary units; accept within half a small square)

hints: Find the top of the first, small peak, then read across.
parts.workedSolution: 20 arbitrary units.

parts.stem: Calculate how many times higher the highest level after the booster is than the highest level after the first dose.

scheme.for: 6.5 (times)

hints: 'How many times' means divide the larger by the smaller.
parts.workedSolution: 130 ÷ 20 = 6.5 times higher.

commonErrors.feedback: That is how much higher, 130 − 20. 'How many times higher' asks for a division: 130 ÷ 20.

parts.stem: Use the graph to explain why the first dose alone did not protect this person.

accepted: the antibody level only reached 20, which is below the level needed for immunity

scheme.for: the antibody level never reached the level needed for immunity
quotes the peak, 20, against 30

hints: Compare the top of the first peak with the dashed line, and quote the number.
parts.workedSolution: After the first dose the antibody level only reached 20, which is below the level of 30 needed for immunity, so it never protected her on its own.

parts.stem: Use the graph to find for how many weeks after the booster the antibody level stayed above the level needed for immunity.

scheme.for: about 17 weeks (from just after week 9 to week 26; accept 16 to 18)

hints: Find where the curve crosses the dashed line going up, and where it crosses going down, then subtract.
parts.workedSolution: The level rises above the line just after week 9 and falls below it at week 26: 26 − 9.1 = about 17 weeks.

commonErrors.feedback: Week 26 is when the level fell below the line, not how long it stayed above it. Subtract the week it rose above the line, just after 9.

the person does not become ill from the vaccine
lymphocytes (white blood cells) recognise its antigens
memory lymphocytes are made and stay in the blood for a long time
when the real pathogen enters, the memory lymphocytes recognise it

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] at least five points, Band B [3]-[4] at least three, Band C [1]-[2] at least one, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Answers that describe how an antibody fits an antigen, without the memory lymphocytes and the faster, larger second response, cap at Band B: the question is about why the vaccinated person stays well. Higher Tier answers may add that a booster raises the antibody and memory lymphocyte levels again.

hints: Tell it as a story in two halves: the injection, then the real infection months later.
The words that lift an answer are modified, antigens, lymphocytes, antibodies, memory lymphocytes, faster and more.
parts.workedSolution: The vaccine contains a modified form of the pathogen, for example a dead or weakened one, so the person does not become ill from it. Lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, recognise its antigens and produce antibodies against them. Memory lymphocytes are also made, and they stay in the blood for a long time. Months later, when the real pathogen enters the body, the memory lymphocytes recognise it at once. Antibodies are produced much faster than the first time, and in greater numbers, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear.

commonErrors.feedback: The fit between antibody and antigen is true but it is not the protection. The marks gather round memory lymphocytes and a second response that is faster and larger.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife measured the clear zone round an antibiotic disc three times: 18 mm, 22 mm, 20 mm. She is asked: 'Calculate the mean clear-zone diameter. [2]'
Her working:
studentWorking: mean = total of the repeats ÷ number of repeats
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 was typed without brackets, so the calculator divided only the last repeat by 3. A mean of 46.7 mm is larger than every repeat, which is impossible.
correction: mean = total of the repeats ÷ number of repeats
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of two: the method in line 1 is right. Brackets put the division last. Then check: 20.0 mm lies between 18 mm and 22 mm, as a mean must.

findTheMistake.stem:
Seán is asked: 'Use the antibody graph to calculate how many times higher the peak after the booster is than the peak after the first dose. [2]'
His working:
studentWorking: peak after the first dose = 24 arbitrary units
peak after the booster = 120 arbitrary units
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 subtracts. 120 − 24 = 96 says how much higher the booster peak is, not how many times higher: 'how many times' is always a division.
correction: peak after the first dose = 24 arbitrary units
peak after the booster = 120 arbitrary units
findTheMistake.feedback: The two readings are right, but the method mark is for the division: 120 ÷ 24 = 5 times higher. A check: 5 × 24 gives back 120.

findings.asked: What a vaccine causes the body to make, and why a second exposure is dealt with faster.
findings.wentWrong: 'Antibodies' was known; the secondary response was described vaguely or as being about the specific fit of antibodies, rather than memory lymphocytes producing antibodies faster and in larger amounts.
findings.rule: Secondary response = memory lymphocytes, faster, more antibodies.

findings.asked: The same vaccination question at Foundation.
findings.wentWrong: Many gave the same vague or misdirected secondary-response answers.
findings.rule: Three ideas: memory cells, quicker, bigger.

findings.asked: Explain, in an unfamiliar predator-prey context, why resistance increased in a population, then give the advantage of the change to the other species.
findings.wentWrong: Natural selection is a topic candidates find difficult: a number drifted into immunity and antibodies instead of the passing on of advantageous genes, and too many gave the effect on the predator when the advantage to the prey was asked for.
findings.rule: Resistance in a population is natural selection - variation, survival, reproduction, allele passed on - not immunity.

findings.asked: Compare antibiotic clear zones and use them as evidence about MRSA.
findings.wentWrong: Picking the best antibiotic was easy, but the reason needed the evidence (largest clear zone, so it killed the most bacteria); a statement that one antibiotic was ineffective against both strains was often missed; and only the more able used the diagram rather than general knowledge about MRSA.
findings.rule: Every judgement from a practical needs the measurement that supports it.

insight.ruleToRemember: A vaccine contains antigens, so lymphocytes make antibodies and memory lymphocytes; on re-infection the response is faster and larger. Antibiotics kill bacteria (not viruses); resistance spreads because resistant bacteria survive and reproduce - natural selection, not immunity.
insight.aStarSignal: Separating three ideas that sound alike - antibody, antibiotic, resistance - and explaining a resistance graph with selection of alleles rather than immunity.
